source.title: 维基百科 · 一號複製人

materials.text: 《一号复制人》（英语：Kid A）是英国另类摇滚乐团电台司令的第四张录音室专辑。专辑于2000年10月发行，旋即横扫全球[1]，发行首周便在英国获得白金唱片[2]。虽然没有发行官方单曲或拍摄音乐视频进行宣传，《一号复制人》仍成为电台司令首张空降美国冠军的专辑作品[3]。

materials.id: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?oldid=1380253010#en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 2
materials.location: en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 2
materials.text: Kid A is the fourth studio album by the English rock band Radiohead, released on 2 October 2000 by Parlophone. It was recorded with their producer, Nigel Godrich, in Paris, Copenhagen, Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire. Departing from their earlier sound, Radiohead incorporated influences from electronic music, krautrock, jazz and 20th-century classical music, with a wider range of instruments and effects. The singer, Thom Yorke, wrote abstract lyrics, cutting up phrases and assembling them at random.

materials.id: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?oldid=1380253010#en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 3
materials.location: en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 3
materials.text: In a departure from industry practice, Radiohead released no singles and conducted few interviews and photoshoots. Instead, they released short animations and became one of the first major acts to use the internet for promotion. Bootlegs of early performances were shared on filesharing services, and Kid A was leaked before release. In 2000, Radiohead toured Europe in a custom-built tent without corporate sponsors.

materials.id: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?oldid=1380253010#en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 4
materials.location: en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 4
materials.text: Kid A debuted at number one on the UK Albums Chart and became Radiohead's first number-one album on the US Billboard 200. It was certified platinum in the UK, the US, Australia, Canada, France and Japan. Its new sound divided listeners, and some dismissed it as pretentious, derivative or wilfully obscure. However, it was later named one of the greatest albums by numerous publications; Rolling Stone, Pitchfork and The Times ranked it the greatest album of the 2000s, and in 2020 Rolling Stone ranked it number 20 on its updated list of the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time. Kid A won the Grammy Award for Best Alternative Album and was nominated for the Grammy Award for Album of the Year.

materials.id: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?oldid=1380253010#en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 5
materials.location: en · Kid A · 导语 · 段落 5
materials.text: Radiohead released a second album of material from the sessions, Amnesiac, in 2001. In 2021, they released Kid A Mnesia, an anniversary reissue compiling Kid A, Amnesiac and previously unreleased material.

materials.location: en · Kid A · Tracks · 段落 17
materials.text: Yorke wrote an early version of "The National Anthem" when the band was still in school.[28] In 1997, Radiohead recorded drums and bass for the song, intending to develop it as a B-side for OK Computer, but decided to keep it for their next album.[28] For Kid A, Greenwood added ondes Martenot and sounds sampled from radio stations,[28] and Yorke's vocals were processed with a ring modulator.[29] In November 1999,[29] Radiohead recorded a brass section inspired by the "organised chaos" of The Complete Town Hall Concert by the jazz musician Charles Mingus, instructing the musicians to sound like a "traffic jam".[30]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Tracks · 段落 20
materials.text: "Motion Picture Soundtrack" was written before Radiohead's debut single, "Creep" (1992),[37] and Radiohead recorded a version on piano during the OK Computer sessions.[38] For Kid A, Yorke recorded it on a pedal organ, influenced by the songwriter Tom Waits. Radiohead added harp samples and double bass, attempting to emulate the soundtracks of 1950s Disney films.[28][39] Radiohead also worked on several songs they did not complete until future albums, including "Nude",[40] "Burn the Witch"[41] and "True Love Waits".[42]

materials.id: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?oldid=1380253010#en · Kid A · Style and influences · 段落 22
materials.location: en · Kid A · Style and influences · 段落 22
materials.text: Kid A incorporates influences from electronic artists on Warp Records[6] such as the 1990s IDM artists Aphex Twin and Autechre;[2] 1970s Krautrock bands such as Can;[6] the jazz of Charles Mingus,[30] Alice Coltrane and Miles Davis;[3] and abstract hip-hop from the Mo'Wax label, including Blackalicious and DJ Krush.[53] Yorke cited Remain in Light (1980) by Talking Heads as a "massive reference point".[54] Björk was another major influence,[55][29] particularly her 1997 album Homogenic,[56] as was the Beta Band.[57] Radiohead attended an Underworld concert which helped renew their enthusiasm in a difficult moment.[58]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Lyrics · 段落 24
materials.text: Yorke's lyrics on Kid A are less personal than on earlier albums, and instead incorporate abstract and surreal themes.[60] He cut up phrases and assembled them at random, combining cliches and banal observations; for example, "Morning Bell" features repeated contrasting lines such as "Where'd you park the car?" and "Cut the kids in half".[61] Yorke described the lyrics as "like shattered bits of mirror ... like pieces of something broken", and said he was not trying to communicate anything specific.[7]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Lyrics · 段落 25
materials.text: Yorke cited David Byrne's approach to lyrics on Remain in Light as an influence: "When they made that record, they had no real songs, just wrote it all as they went along. Byrne turned up with pages and pages, and just picked stuff up and threw bits in all the time. And that's exactly how I approached Kid A."[3] Radiohead used Yorke's lyrics "like pieces in a collage ... [creating] an artwork out of a lot of different little things".[6] The lyrics are not included in the liner notes, as Radiohead felt they could not be considered independently of the music,[62] and Yorke did not want listeners to focus on them.[3]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Lyrics · 段落 26
materials.text: Yorke wrote "Everything in Its Right Place" about the depression he experienced on the OK Computer tour, feeling he could not speak.[63] The refrain of "How to Disappear Completely" was inspired by R.E.M. singer Michael Stipe, who advised Yorke to relieve tour stress by repeating to himself: "I'm not here, this isn't happening".[64] The refrain of "Optimistic" ("try the best you can / the best you can is good enough") was an assurance by Yorke's partner, Rachel Owen, when Yorke was frustrated with the band's progress.[6] The title Kid A came from a filename on one of Yorke's sequencers.[7] Yorke said he liked its "non-meaning", saying: "If you call [an album] something specific, it drives the record in a certain way."[5]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Artwork · 段落 27
materials.text: The Kid A artwork and packaging was created by Yorke with Stanley Donwood, who has worked with Radiohead since their 1994 EP My Iron Lung.[65] Whereas the pair had previously created album artwork through collage, photography and digital manipulation, for Kid A they used paint for the first time. Donwood used canvases measuring six square feet. He painted on them with knives and sticks and used Artex to create textured surfaces, which Yorke photographed and manipulated with Photoshop.[66][67] Donwood focused on painting, while Yorke focused on digital editing.[66] While working on the artwork, Yorke and Donwood became "obsessed" with the Worldwatch Institute website, which was full of "scary statistics about ice caps melting, and weather patterns changing"; this inspired them to use an image of a mountain range as the cover art.[68] Donwood said he saw the mountains as "some sort of cataclysmic power".[69]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Artwork · 段落 29
materials.text: Yorke and Donwood made many versions of the album cover, with different pictures and different titles in different typefaces. Unable to pick one, they taped them to cupboards of the studio kitchen and went to bed. According to Donwood, the choice the next day "was obvious".[72] In October 2021, Yorke and Donwood curated an exhibition of Kid A artwork at Christie's headquarters in London.[73]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Promotion · 段落 30
materials.text: Radiohead minimised their involvement in promotion for Kid A,[78] conducting few interviews or photoshoots.[79] Though "Optimistic" and promotional copies of other tracks received radio play, Radiohead released no singles from the album. Yorke said this was to avoid the stress of publicity, which he had struggled with on OK Computer, rather than for artistic reasons.[78] He later said he regretted the decision, feeling it meant much of the early judgement of the album came from critics.[78]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Promotion · 段落 31
materials.text: Radiohead were careful to present Kid A as a cohesive work rather than a series of separate tracks. Rather than give EMI executives their own copies, they had them listen to the album in its entirety on a bus from Hollywood to Malibu.[80] The Independent journalist Nick Haze said it was "delivered to journalists like Holy Writ".[81] Rob Gordon, the vice president of marketing at Capitol Records, the American subsidiary of Radiohead's label EMI, praised the album but said promoting it would be a "business challenge".[82]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Promotion · 段落 32
materials.text: No advance copies of Kid A were circulated,[83] but it was played under controlled conditions for critics and fans.[84] On September 5, 2000, it was played for the public for the first time at the IMAX theatre in Lincoln Square, Manhattan.[85] Promotional copies of Kid A came with stickers prohibiting broadcast before September 19. At midnight, it was played in its entirety by the London radio station Xfm.[86] MTV2,[87] KROQ, and WXRK also played the album.[2]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Videos · 段落 34
materials.text: Instead of releasing traditional music videos for Kid A, Radiohead commissioned dozens of 10-second videos featuring Donwood artwork they called "blips", which were aired on music channels and distributed online.[89] Pitchfork described them as "context-free animated nightmares that radiated mystery", with "arch hints of surveillance".[90] Five of the videos were serviced as exclusives to MTV, and "helped play into the arty mystique that endeared Radiohead to its core audience", according to Billboard.[91] Much of the promotional material featured pointy-toothed bear characters created by Donwood. The bears originated in stories Donwood made for his young children about teddy bears who came to life and ate the "grown-ups" who had abandoned them.[72]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Internet · 段落 35
materials.text: Everything in the industry at that point was like, "The internet isn't important. It's not selling records" – everything for them had to translate to a sale. I knew the internet was [generating sales], but I couldn't prove it because every record had MTV and radio with it. [After Kid A was a success], nobody in the industry could believe it because there was no radio and there was no traditional music video. I knew at that point: this is the story of the internet. The internet has done this.

materials.location: en · Kid A · Internet · 段落 37
materials.text: To promote Kid A, Capitol created the "iBlip", a Java applet that could be embedded in fan sites. It allowed users to stream the album, and included artwork, photos and links to order Kid A on Amazon.[82][80] It was used by more than 1000 sites, and the album was streamed more than 400,000 times.[80] Capitol also streamed Kid A through Amazon, MTV.com and heavy.com, and ran a campaign with the peer-to-peer filesharing service Aimster, allowing users to swap iBlips and Radiohead-branded Aimster skins.[82]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Internet · 段落 38
materials.text: Three weeks before release, Kid A was leaked online and shared on the peer-to-peer service Napster. Asked whether he believed Napster had damaged sales, the Capitol president, Ray Lott, likened the situation to unfounded concern about home taping in the 1980s and said: "I'm trying to sell as many Radiohead albums as possible. If I worried about what Napster would do, I wouldn't sell as many albums."[82] Yorke said Napster "encourages enthusiasm for music in a way that the music industry has long forgotten to do".[93]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Internet · 段落 39
materials.text: The commercial success of Kid A suggested that leaks might not be as damaging as many had assumed.[94] The music journalist Brent DiCrescenzo argued that the Napster leak profoundly affected the way Kid A was received, surprising listeners who would patiently download new tracks to find they comprised "four minutes of ambient noise".[91]

materials.location: en · Kid A · Tour · 段落 40
materials.text: Radiohead rearranged the Kid A songs to perform them live. O'Brien said, "You couldn't do Kid A live and be true to the record. You would have to do it like an art installation ... When we played live, we put the human element back into it."[95] Selway said they "found some new life" in the songs when they came to perform them.[95] Yorke said: "Even with electronics, there is an element of spontaneous performance in using them ... It was the tension between what's human and what's coming from the machines. That was stuff we were getting into, as we learned how to play the songs from Kid A and Amnesiac live."[96]
